title: Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain
summary: The Hawaiian–Emperor chain is a line of more than 125 volcanoes stretching about 3,720 miles across the North Pacific. Its northernmost Emperor seamounts are estimated at about 80 million years old. A bend between the two segments was dated to 42.0 ± 1.4 million years, and the bend is attributed to a change in Pacific plate motion, though later work stresses hotspot-ridge effects.

uncertainty.note: Start is the estimate for the northern Emperor seamounts (about 80 million years, USGS Volcano Watch). End is the bend age 42.0 ± 1.4 m.y. (Dalrymple and Clague 1976); USGS Volcano Watch gives about 43 million years. The Hawaiian segment formed after the bend.

when.display: Emperor segment c. 80 to 42 million years ago

where.modern_name: Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain, North Pacific (pin at the Hawaii end of the chain)
where.historical_name: Seafloor of the central and northern Pacific; no polities

paleo.not_applicable: The chain is a hotspot track, not a plate-fixed site; the pin marks the Hawaii end of the chain, and reconstructing its modern coordinate to 80 Ma would not describe the volcanoes.

importance.justification: A hotspot track used to reconstruct Pacific plate motion; its bend is a long-debated marker.
